Hermann Oberth. Austro-Hungarian physicist who published the pioneering treatise Die Rakete zu den Planetenräumen — The Rocket into Planetary Space — in 1923. This work synthesized theoretical rocketry and astronautics, providing the intellectual bridge between Tsiolkovsky's equations and engineering practice.

His book argued rigorously that liquid-fueled multi-stage rockets could reach the moon and beyond — a feat deemed impossible by the scientific mainstream. Working independently of Tsiolkovsky and Goddard, his book became the manifesto of German rocketry societies and drew young engineers, including von Braun, into spaceflight. Oberth conceived of rocket-powered spaceflight to Mars, space mirrors to focus solar energy on Earth, and other ambitious schemes that were purely theoretical but scientifically reasoned.

He struggled to secure funding and institutional support in Germany and later Romania. Despite his brilliance, he remained a marginal figure in engineering circles until late in life. After World War II, like von Braun, he emigrated to the United States and continued publishing on space propulsion and extraterrestrial colonization into his nineties.

His work was cited by von Braun and the German rocket societies as a key inspiration. Soviet engineers also read him and credited his influence on their own theoretical framework.
